title: Classification and Exact Local Masking in Finite-Field Clifford Dual-Unitary Circuits
abstract: We classify two-qudit finite-field Clifford dual-unitary gates and apply the classification to exact local masking and operator transport in homogeneous brickwork circuits. Under ordered one-qudit Clifford equivalence, the dual-unitary locus contains $q-2$ perfect-tensor cores, one rank-one core, and one SWAP core. The perfect cores are indexed by \[ δ=\det B=\det C, \] and are related to the ordered cross-ratio $λ$ of the associated $[4,2,3]_q$ MDS configuration through \[ λ=\fracδ{δ-1}. \] Homogeneous repetition separates these cores into five transport phases whose algebraic codimensions in $\operatorname{Sp}(4,q)$ are $0,1,2,3,4$.   The one-site Weyl edge channels determine exact local-masking distances. Perfect-tensor circuits attain \[ d_1(t)=4t, \qquad d_2(t)=4t-2, \] whereas delayed erasers satisfy \[ d_1(t)=4t-2, \qquad d_2(t)=4t-4 \] for $t\geq 2$. Consequently, sufficiently short quantum messages are completely hidden from every one- or two-qudit output subsystem, even when the input is entangled with a reference, while remaining exactly recoverable from the full output.   For $q=3$, we construct an explicit perfect-tensor Clifford gate from two inverse SUM gates. Exhaustive Weyl-support searches for $t=1,2,3$ reproduce the predicted masking distances, and a one-period Choi-channel calculation for a four-qutrit periodic circuit gives numerical residual leakage below $2\times 10^{-16}$. Under the coherent perturbation considered here, local leakage is linear in the perturbation strength, whereas the infidelity of recovery using the ideal inverse is quadratic near the perfect point.
summary: This theoretical paper classifies complex two-qudit gates within finite fields by analyzing their structure using symplectic groups. It establishes precise quantitative bounds on 'local masking'—the ability to hide input information from subsets of output qubits while retaining full recoverability. This has significant implications for designing secure quantum communication protocols.
main_problem: The paper classifies two-qudit finite-field Clifford dual-unitary gates and applies this classification to determine exact local masking properties in homogeneous brickwork quantum circuits.
main_result: It proves that sufficiently short quantum messages can be completely hidden from any one- or two-qudit output subsystem, even when the input is entangled, while remaining perfectly recoverable from the full output.
method: The analysis uses symplectic matrix representations over finite fields ($\mathbb{F}_q$) to classify gate loci and employs concepts like local masking distances derived from Weyl edge channels.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum circuits built using two-qudit gates defined over finite fields, specifically analyzing the structure of dual-unitary Clifford elements within $	ext{Sp}(4, q)$.
key_observables: Local masking distances ($d_1(t), d_2(t)$); symplectic core types ($S_\delta$, $SR$, $SS$); and recovery fidelities.
important_parameters: The finite field size $q$; circuit depth $t$; and the determinant parameter $\delta$.
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes between local gate equivalence and homogeneous circuit transport, and assumes specific boundary conditions for edge channel analysis.
figures_summary: Tables summarize exact phase counts for different edge-transport phases within the dual-unitary symplectic classes; diagrams illustrate core structures related to cross-ratios.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the finite-field Clifford representation, classifying dual-unitary gates and perfect tensors using symplectic invariants, developing the concept of masking distances via Weyl channels, and finally applying these results to derive specific local privacy guarantees.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools (symplectic geometry, algebraic combinatorics) to quantify quantum information security primitives like data hiding and local observability in structured quantum computation models.
